8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":7,"verseId":12,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Arising, Abiding, and Ceasing","totalVerses":34,"verseData":{"id":"v7_12","number":12,"title":"The Symmetry Argument","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If lamplight illuminated itself and that of others, darkness too would without doubt obscure itself and the thing of others."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The final blow to the lamp analogy: if light has the inherent power to illuminate itself AND others, then by symmetry, darkness should have the inherent power to conceal itself AND others. But darkness doesn't conceal itself — we can perceive darkness. The symmetry fails, proving the opponent's model of inherent self-affecting properties is incoherent.","madhyamaka":"If illumination is an inherent property of light (affecting both self and others), then concealment should be an inherent property of darkness (affecting both self and others). But darkness is perceivable — it doesn't conceal itself. Therefore, self-affecting inherent properties don't work. Garfield: \"The symmetry argument is the most elegant refutation of the lamp analogy.\"","quantum":"Symmetry principles are foundational in physics: CPT symmetry, gauge symmetries, Noether's theorem. If a property holds for one member of a symmetric pair, it should hold for the other. Nāgārjuna applies this reasoning: if self-affecting properties are real, the symmetry between light and darkness should be maintained.","bridge":"Both Nāgārjuna and physics rely on symmetry to test claims. If a principle works for light but fails for its opposite (darkness), it's not a genuine inherent property — it's an artifact of selective reasoning. Broken symmetry in physics often reveals deeper structure; here it reveals emptiness.","accessible":"If \"hot\" inherently warms itself and others, then \"cold\" should inherently cool itself and others. But does darkness \"darken\" itself? We can see darkness — it's visible! So it doesn't conceal itself. The symmetry breaks, showing the whole model is flawed.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, light illuminates and darkness obscures — they work differently. The opponent tried to make self-illumination an INHERENT property. But inherent properties should be symmetric, and they're not. Convention works; inherent properties don't.","commonMisconception":"NOT claiming light and darkness are identical. Claiming that IF self-affecting is an inherent property of one, it should be an inherent property of its opposite. Since it's not, self-affecting inherent properties don't exist for either."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Symmetry Principles in Physics","score":74,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Symmetry principles (CPT, gauge, Noether's theorem) require that properties holding for one member of a symmetric pair hold for the counterpart. Nāgārjuna applies this: if self-illumination is inherent to light, self-concealment should be inherent to darkness. The asymmetry disproves inherent self-affecting properties.","caveat":"Physical symmetries are precise mathematical relationships. Nāgārjuna's symmetry argument is conceptual, not mathematical. The parallel is about the principle of symmetric reasoning."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A split screen: light on one side (supposedly self-illuminating), darkness on the other (should be self-concealing). But the darkness is visible — the symmetry breaks. Visualizes the argument's elegance.","educationalGoal":"User sees that the symmetry between light and darkness breaks when applied to self-affecting properties, disproving the opponent's model."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why should darkness behave symmetrically to light?","a":"If illumination is an INHERENT property of light (not dependent on conditions), then concealment should be an inherent property of darkness. Inherent properties are essential, not contingent. If the model works for one, symmetry demands it work for the other.","realLifeExample":"If \"being wet\" is an inherent property of water, then \"being dry\" should be an inherent property of sand. Testing the claim on both members of a pair reveals if it's truly inherent."},{"q":"What's wrong with darkness concealing itself?","a":"If darkness concealed itself, we couldn't perceive it at all — it would be invisible even as darkness. But we DO perceive darkness. We experience dark rooms, shadows, nighttime. Darkness is phenomenally present to us, proving it doesn't conceal itself.","realLifeExample":"If silence \"silenced\" itself, you wouldn't notice silence at all. But you DO notice silence — it's a distinct experience. So silence doesn't \"silence\" itself."},{"q":"How does this complete the critique of the lamp analogy?","a":"V.9: Self-illumination fails (no darkness to dispel). V.10: Interaction mechanism is unlocatable. V.11: Without interaction, effects are absurdly universal. V.12: Symmetry with darkness breaks. ALL four angles of the lamp analogy collapse. Self-causation has no viable model.","realLifeExample":"A fortress attacked from all four sides: north wall breached (v.9), east wall (v.10), west wall (v.11), south wall (v.12). The fortress (lamp analogy) falls completely."},{"q":"What are symmetry principles in physics?","a":"CPT symmetry (charge-parity-time reversal), gauge symmetries, and Noether's theorem all state that physical laws respect certain symmetries. If a property holds in one context, symmetry demands it hold in the transformed context. Nāgārjuna applies analogous reasoning to the light/darkness pair.","realLifeExample":"If driving on the right is mandatory, then for symmetry's sake, the opposite rule (driving on the left) should work just as well in mirror-image countries — and indeed it does (UK vs US)."},{"q":"Does this mean light and darkness are the same?","a":"No. Nāgārjuna is NOT equating them. He's testing whether \"self-affecting\" is an inherent property. If it is, it should apply symmetrically. It doesn't, so it's not inherent. Light and darkness remain conventionally distinct; they just don't have inherent self-affecting natures.","realLifeExample":"Testing whether \"self-cleaning\" is inherent to soap by asking if dirt should be \"self-dirtying.\" They're different things; the test reveals the property isn't inherent."},{"q":"What is the broader implication for the chapter?","a":"With the lamp analogy demolished (vv.8-12), the opponent has exhausted three strategies for grounding inherent arising: infinite regress (v.3), circular dependency (vv.4-6), and self-causation via the lamp (vv.8-12). All fail. The chapter will now analyze abiding and ceasing (vv.25-32) and draw final conclusions (vv.33-34).","deeper":"The lamp analogy section also establishes a template Nāgārjuna uses in other chapters — particularly his analysis of perception (MMK Ch.3) and fire/fuel (MMK Ch.10), where similar self-reference arguments apply."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What does Nāgārjuna's symmetry argument show?","options":["A) Light and darkness are identical","B) If light self-illuminates (inherently), darkness should self-conceal, but it doesn't — so self-affecting properties aren't inherent","C) Darkness is more powerful than light","D) Symmetry doesn't matter in philosophy"],"correct":"B","explanation":"If self-illumination is inherent to light, self-concealment should be inherent to darkness. But darkness doesn't conceal itself (we perceive it). So self-affecting inherent properties don't exist."},"intermediate":{"question":"Why doesn't darkness conceal itself?","options":["A) It does conceal itself","B) We perceive darkness — dark rooms, shadows, night. If it concealed itself, it would be imperceptible.","C) Darkness is too weak","D) Only light has inherent properties"],"correct":"B","explanation":"We directly experience darkness. If darkness inherently concealed itself, we couldn't perceive it at all. Since we do, self-concealment is not an inherent property of darkness."},"advanced":{"question":"How does the symmetry argument connect to broader Mādhyamika philosophy?","options":["A) It doesn't connect","B) It demonstrates that no phenomena have inherent self-affecting properties, supporting the universal emptiness of svabhāva","C) It proves only light is empty","D) Symmetry only applies to physics"],"correct":"B","explanation":"By showing self-affecting properties fail for both light and darkness, Nāgārjuna generalizes: no phenomenon has inherent properties that determine its behavior independently of conditions. This supports universal emptiness."}},"verseText":"If lamplight illuminated itself and that of others, darkness too would without doubt obscure itself and the thing of others.","madhyamakaConcept":"If illumination is an inherent property of light (affecting both self and others), then concealment should be an inherent property of darkness (affecting both self and others).
